title: Welcome to RTcode
summary: A small, deliberate home for your code. This is your operator’s guide.

blocks.text: Find your bearings

The top strip identifies your workspace and places terminal layout, commands, and Settings within reach. Files, Search, and Git live on the left. Your code stays in one central editor group. The status strip shows document position, language, save state, and trust.
Start a session

Choose the workspace name or Open a workspace to select a local folder. Browse files immediately in Restricted Mode. Trust only folders whose contents you understand before starting a terminal or formatter.
Help stays close
The R_> logo always returns here. F1 does the same. Settings opens over your workbench: editor models and terminals remain alive. Escape or Back to editor restores your context.
An honest early build

This version implements a local editing workbench. The browser preview uses sample files in memory. It cannot launch shells or read your computer. Read Updates and limitations for the implementation boundary.

title: Workspaces & trust
summary: Open a folder safely. Decide when its code may execute.

blocks.text: Open a workspace

The desktop app automatically opens the directory it was launched from. Click the workspace control in the top bar to see open folders. The Add workspace button stays at the bottom of the dropdown and opens the native folder picker. Adding a folder keeps existing files, unsaved edits, and terminals open. Selecting an already open folder does not duplicate it. Use the × beside a folder in the dropdown to remove it from the workbench. Its files and terminals close; the folder stays on disk. Modified files offer Save all & remove, Don’t save & remove, or Cancel. Running terminals require confirmation. Other workspaces stay open.

All workspace roots appear as separate, collapsible folders in Files. Each workspace has its own highlight color around its root name and along its open editor tabs. The dropdown selects the workspace used for Search, Git, new files, and the trust control. File tabs keep their own workspace association.

Selecting a worktree in Git asks whether to Add workspace or Replace workspace. Replace affects only the selected workspace, closes its files and terminals, and prompts to save or discard unsaved edits. Cancel leaves it unchanged. A failed save or unavailable destination preserves the current workspace.

On macOS, a fresh launch with open -a 'RTcode' uses the shell's current folder. If RTcode is already running, that command only activates it; use the workspace picker or open -n -a 'RTcode' for a new instance from the current folder.
Restricted mode

File browsing, editing, search, and read-only Git are available. Terminals, SSH, formatting, and Git mutations are blocked. The bottom-left trust control reviews the exact canonical folder before granting access.
Revoke trust

Settings → Security can revoke trust and end that workspace’s active terminal sessions. Exact-root trust is stored locally. Parent trust and automatic workspace restoration are not implemented in this build.

title: Files & editing
summary: A single editor group. Reliable saves. Explicit failure.

blocks.text: Open and edit

The explorer lists every entry in a folder, including dotfiles and paths ignored by Git such as node_modules, with no entry-count limit. Select a file from the tree to open a tab. Monaco provides undo, find, multiple cursors, and syntax highlighting. A dot marks unsaved changes. Save with Cmd/Ctrl+S. Closing a dirty tab requires an explicit discard decision.
Safe save

The native service checks the on-disk content hash before saving, writes a temporary file in the same directory, preserves permissions, then persists the replacement. Failure leaves your buffer dirty. A conflict requires explicit overwrite. Compare and Save As are pending.
Formats and limits

UTF-8, a UTF-8 BOM, and consistent LF/CRLF endings are preserved. Binary or unsupported encodings fail explicitly. Files above 10 MiB are rejected in this early build instead of risking an unbounded load. New files can be created in the root. Rename and trash backend operations are not yet exposed in the explorer.
Current tab behavior
Every open file is pinned in this build. Preview tabs, automatic external-change reload, recovery buffers, and session restoration are pending. Keep important edits saved before quitting.

title: Workspace search
summary: Find text on demand, without a permanent content index.

blocks.text: Search a folder

Choose Search, enter a query, and press Enter or the Search button. Nothing is searched while you type; after you change the query or an option, the results are marked STALE until you search again, and Replace all stays disabled. Aa enables case sensitivity, ab enables whole-word matching, and .* enables regular expressions. Include and exclude fields accept comma-separated glob patterns, such as src/**, **/*.{ts,tsx}. A plain folder name matches that folder at any depth; prefix ./ to anchor it to the workspace root. Invalid expressions and filters appear inline.
Find files by name

The icon at the left of the search field switches modes. The magnifying glass marks the content filter described above. Select it to switch to file search, marked by the files icon, and the include, exclude, and replace controls disappear because they apply only to content filtering. Enter part of a file name and press Enter or Search; every space-separated term must appear somewhere in the file's path, ignoring case. Exact names sort first, then names starting with the query, names containing it, and finally paths that match elsewhere. Only the best 200 matches are listed, with a note giving the total, so add more of the name or path to narrow them. Select a result to open that file. File search respects .gitignore and .ignore and lists dotfiles. The typed text is kept when switching modes, but the results are cleared.
Limits

Search runs inside the desktop app without an external executable. It respects .gitignore and .ignore, and skips hidden files, symlinks, and binary/non-UTF-8 files. Content search has no time, file-size, line-length, query/filter-length, or result-count limit. Long result previews are shortened around each match; the full line is searched. A new request cancels the previous search. Select a result to jump to the highlighted UTF-16 editor range. Search reads saved files; save edits to include them. The Rust regex engine supports captures and Unicode matching, but not lookaround or backreferences in patterns.
Replace matches

Select Replace to show the replacement field. Use the arrow beside a result to replace one match, or Replace all to replace the current complete result set. Empty replacement text deletes matches. In regex mode, $1 and ${name} insert capture groups; $$ inserts a literal dollar sign. In literal mode, replacement text is used as typed.

Review the match/file count before confirming. Save or close modified matching tabs first. Each file is checked against its search revision and saved atomically, preserving BOM and line endings. Changed or unwritable files are skipped with visible errors; successful files are reported and open buffers refresh. A multi-file replacement is not one atomic transaction and is limited to 64 MiB of updated content. Opening and replacing matching files still uses the 10 MiB editor file limit. Browser samples replace only in-memory sample content.

title: Minimal Git
summary: Inspect the repository. Stage deliberately. Keep advanced workflows in the terminal.

blocks.text: Repository state

The Git tab shows the current branch, worktrees, local and remote refs separately, the ten most recent commits, and staged and unstaged changes. Worktrees are expanded by default; other sections start collapsed. Select a section header to expand or collapse it. Refresh re-reads the repository. The sample preview does not fabricate repository data.
Switch worktrees

Worktrees show their branch (or detached commit), full path, and current, locked, or unavailable state. Select an available worktree to make it the workspace. A locked worktree can still be opened; missing, prunable, and bare entries cannot. RTcode verifies that the destination still belongs to the repository before switching.

Unsaved editor changes prompt Save all & switch, Don’t save & switch, or Cancel. Cancel is focused by default. Save all includes inactive tabs; failed or conflicting saves keep the current workspace open. Discarding applies only after the destination opens successfully. Saved but uncommitted changes stay in their original worktree. Active terminal sessions close during a confirmed switch. The destination uses its own saved trust decision. Worktree creation, removal, and pruning remain terminal workflows.
Changes and diffs

Select a changed or staged filename to open the editable working file. Select the eye button beside it to open the corresponding read-only patch. Deleted files can still be inspected with the eye button. Plus stages a file; minus unstages it. Both require trust. Conflicted paths have mutations disabled. No automatic stash, fetch, or discard runs.
Branch switching

Select a local branch and review the action. Git refuses switches that would overwrite changes. Remote tracking-branch creation remains a terminal workflow in this build. There is no commit, push, pull, merge, rebase, or stash UI.
Unusual repositories

Detached and unborn states have explicit labels. Repositories and linked worktrees rooted at the selected folder are discovered. Parent repositories, advanced submodule UI, and cross-platform worktree certification remain pending.

title: Terminal
summary: A real PTY in the desktop app. Start it when you need it.

blocks.text: Start a shell

Trust the workspace, then press Start a terminal or the plus button. With multiple workspaces open, a picker asks which folder to use. Cancel starts nothing. The shell runs in the chosen workspace root, and its tab includes that workspace’s name. Restricted folders require trust before starting. Up to eight tabs are available. The browser preview cannot start a shell.

New Unix shells are interactive, non-login sessions. Your interactive startup files still load (for example, .zshrc or .bashrc), while login-only profiles are not rerun for each tab. Shells inherit the app's environment. Tools configured only in login profiles must be available in that environment or configured in your interactive startup file. Slow interactive plugins can still delay the first prompt.
Move the terminal

Use the independent RIGHT and BOTTOM toggles in TERM// to show either terminal pane or both. Each pane has its own sessions. HIDE, or the hide button in either pane, hides both without ending sessions. Re-enabling a pane restores its existing xterm instances and backend PTYs. Resizing sends the final dimensions after a short debounce. Hidden terminals continue running.
Input and security

Terminal focus sends keystrokes to the shell. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette as an escape chord. OSC 52 clipboard writes are suppressed. No transcripts or input are stored. Shell environment inheritance occurs only after trust.
Closing

The terminal header close control ends the active session after confirmation. Closing the app or replacing a workspace also asks before ending its live sessions. Adding or selecting a workspace keeps existing sessions running. The backend kills its owned PTY children. Graceful descendant cleanup across all operating systems requires further validation.

title: SSH connections
summary: Use the system OpenSSH client and its familiar authentication prompts.

blocks.text: Connect
Open SSH in the bottom strip, enter a config alias or user@host, and select Connect. A trusted workspace is required. The backend launches ssh directly in a PTY, with an argument vector.
Authentication

Keys, agents, passwords, ProxyJump, and host-key prompts are handled by OpenSSH. Unknown host keys require your normal decision; changed keys are not accepted automatically. No secrets or transcripts are stored.
Connection state

The UI reports that an SSH process is running. It does not infer authenticated connection success from terminal text. Exit ends the session. Favorites, Include-file discovery, disconnect escalation, and editing SSH config through an external document handle remain pending.
Remote scope
An SSH terminal is not a remote workspace. Files, search, Git, and formatting still operate locally. Remote workspace development is a separate future architecture.

title: Languages & IntelliSense
summary: Completion, hints, navigation, and real diagnostics from bundled language services.

blocks.text: Built-in language services

TypeScript and JavaScript use Monaco's bundled TypeScript service for completion, hover types, signature help, inlay hints, definitions, references, symbol rename, quick fixes, and syntax/type diagnostics. JSON includes syntax validation and completion. CSS, SCSS, and Less include validation and completion. HTML includes completion and hover help; this is not a complete HTML linter.
These services run locally in dedicated workers. They do not execute project scripts or require workspace trust. Remote JSON schema fetching is disabled.
Using hints and diagnostics

Ctrl+Space requests completion. Hover a symbol to inspect its type. Parameter hints appear while entering function calls. F12 goes to a definition and F2 renames supported symbols. The editor context menu offers the language actions available at the current cursor. Lightbulbs offer available quick fixes.

Errors are red; warnings, diagnostic hints, and inline type/parameter hints are yellow. These colors apply to the editor and Problems independently of the accent palette. Select the status bar's diagnostic counts, or press Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+M, to open Problems. Select a problem to jump to its file and location. F8 and Shift+F8 navigate diagnostics within the editor. Diagnostics update as you type and disappear when the problem is fixed.
Scope and project configuration

The desktop app loads workspace sources, JSON configs, and installed dependency declarations on demand. TypeScript reads tsconfig.json or jsconfig.json (including JSON comments, extends, baseUrl, paths, include/exclude, and module resolution settings). Nested projects keep their own configurations; solution configs can refer to app-specific configs. Package metadata supplies types and exports. Imports and Go to Definition work for files you have not opened, because the language service asks for them when it needs them. Unsaved open buffers take precedence over files on disk. Symbol rename requires all affected files to be open so every changed buffer can be reviewed and saved.

There is no project snapshot. When you open a file, the language service looks for the configs above it and for the files it imports, and only those are read from disk, a few at a time, until nothing is missing. Files you never import are never read, so large workspaces and node_modules cost nothing until something uses them. Editing an import loads the new target shortly after you stop typing. Loaded files refresh after saving and when the app regains focus. The status bar shows INDEXING while files load, then PROJECT, or PARTIAL if loading stopped early, or INDEX ERROR. Symlinks outside the workspace are not read. Dependencies must already be installed. Packages installed later are found when the app regains focus; Reload project configuration in the command palette also drops dependency files that were already loaded, for example after upgrading one. Whole-project features such as references or diagnostics for files you have not opened only cover files that have been loaded. Browser samples still use bundled defaults and open files.

This uses the bundled TypeScript version, not a project's custom compiler or executable plugins. Framework-generated types must exist on disk; Svelte/Vue plugins and ESLint are not loaded. These checks do not replace your project's compiler, tests, or lint command.

Rust, Python, Go, Java, and other languages retain syntax highlighting. Their semantic intelligence requires external language servers, which are not yet integrated. The status bar distinguishes project TypeScript support, BUILT-IN services, and SYNTAX ONLY. VS Code extension and language-server parity is not claimed.
Formatting

Format Document uses a configured external formatter when present. Otherwise it tries the active language's built-in formatter. External processes require a trusted workspace; bundled formatters run locally without executing workspace tools.

title: Formatting
summary: Configure an installed formatter, then apply one undoable edit.

blocks.text: Configure a provider

Settings → Languages & Format accepts an executable and a JSON argument array. The formatter receives document text on stdin and returns replacement text on stdout. The {file} placeholder is replaced inside each argument; no shell expansion occurs.
Run and recover

Press FORMAT or Shift+Alt+F. External formatters require a trusted workspace, have a ten-second runtime cap, and bounded output. If the document or version changes while formatting, the response is discarded. Failures preserve your buffer. Format-on-save and LSP priority are pending.
Example arguments
For an installed prettier executable, set the argument array to ["--stdin-filepath", "{file}"]. This example is configuration text, not a Run button.
Built-in formatting
When no external formatter is configured, Format Document tries the bundled formatter for the active language. External formatters take precedence when configured.

title: Extensions
summary: No blanket VS Code compatibility claim.

blocks.text: Current support
VSIX installation and contribution registration are not implemented in this early build. No extension JavaScript runs. Do not place untrusted extension code in the application source.
Compatibility contract

The intended first tier contains only allowlisted declarative themes, snippets, and language metadata. Grammars need a separate CSP and size spike. Browser extensions are conditional. Node-only extensions require a larger architecture decision.
Sources and licenses

The application does not contact the Visual Studio Marketplace. Future user-supplied VSIX packages must be inspected for archive safety, contribution compatibility, source, hash, and license before an explicit install action.

title: Appearance & layout
summary: One coherent console, from code to documentation.

blocks.text: The console system

Retro 82 uses dark engineered layers, warm amber command signals, cool teal live signals, hairlines, square geometry, and monospace typography. No scanlines, animated backgrounds, or glowing code text obscure work.
Personalization

Settings → Editor controls font size, word wrap, and minimap. Appearance offers high contrast, restrained motion, and editable base colors for the primary accent, secondary accent, background, surface, and text. Defaults use orange and teal. Color changes apply immediately to the workbench, R_> logo, editor, and live terminals. Reset colors restores the default palette. System reduced-motion preference is respected. Terminal placement is controlled in the top toolbar.
Responsive layout

The minimum desktop window is 820 × 560. Below 1000 px terminals move below the editor; when both panes are enabled they share that bottom row and the sidebar becomes a rail with a focus-open overlay. Resize separators support arrow keys.

title: Settings reference
summary: Typed preferences stored as metadata in native SQLite.

blocks.text: Editor settings
fontSize: number, default 13, range 10–28. wrap: boolean, default false. minimap: boolean, default false. All apply immediately at user scope.
Appearance settings

contrast: boolean, default false. motion: boolean, default true. colors: base-color object with primary accent #faa968 (orange), secondary accent #5db7a5 (teal), background #0b0f14, surface #111821, and text #e7dccb. Colors persist with native user preferences; browser preview colors last for the current page session. All apply immediately. Operating-system reduced motion overrides motion effects.
Tools and layout

formatter: executable string, default empty. formatterArgs: JSON string array, default []. Execution requires trust. layout stores terminal placement and pane extents. These settings do not store source buffers or terminal content.
Storage

Native preferences and exact-root trust live in the app-data SQLite database. Browser preview preferences last only for the page session. Workspace-specific overrides, export, sync, reset, and migration recovery UI are pending.

title: Keyboard reference
summary: Use Cmd on macOS and Ctrl on Windows and Linux.

blocks.text: Workbench
F1: open Settings → Guide. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P: command palette. Cmd/Ctrl+O: open folder. Cmd/Ctrl+S: save. Cmd/Ctrl+W: close active tab. Cmd/Ctrl+B: toggle sidebar.
Tools

Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E: Files. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+F: Search. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+G: Git. Cmd/Ctrl+J: hide/show terminal. Cmd/Ctrl+backtick: focus terminal. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+backtick: new terminal. Shift+Alt+F: format. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+M: Problems. Ctrl+Space: completion. F12: definition. F2: rename. F8/Shift+F8: next/previous diagnostic. Language-specific actions require a supported language service.
Navigation

Tab moves between controls. Enter and Space activate buttons, including RTcode. Escape closes Settings or a dialog. Arrow keys on splitters resize panes. Cmd/Ctrl+F in Guide focuses its search field. Editable bindings and several planned advanced shortcuts remain pending.

title: Security & privacy
summary: Rust owns authority. The webview requests narrow operations.

blocks.text: Workspace scope

Opaque workspace, document, and path IDs scope native file commands. Paths are validated and canonicalized under the workspace root. Symlink directory traversal is disabled. The main webview has no generic shell, filesystem, or SQL capability.
Execution

Terminals, SSH, formatters, and Git mutations require workspace trust checked in Rust. Children use executable and argument arrays. Read-only Git disables external diff/textconv and filesystem monitor helpers.
Local data

SQLite stores metadata and settings only. No passwords, private keys, passphrases, file buffers, terminal input, or transcripts enter it. Telemetry is absent. The Guide contains bundled static data and no executable Markdown.
Release status

This is a development build, not a security-audited release. Remaining hardening includes race-resistant directory handles, platform process-group cleanup, archive defenses, updater signatures, and the full cross-platform threat test matrix.

title: Troubleshooting & recovery
summary: Failures should preserve your work and explain the next step.

blocks.text: Missing tool

tool_missing means the executable was not found. Install Git, OpenSSH, or your formatter separately and restart the app so PATH is refreshed. Workspace search is built in and does not need ripgrep. The IDE does not download executables.
Save failures

conflict means disk content changed since the load or last save. Cancel to preserve both versions until you decide. permission_denied and internal errors leave the buffer dirty. Copy the buffer before closing if the filesystem cannot be repaired.
PTY and formatter failures

workspace_untrusted requires reviewing trust. tool_failed means the child exited unsuccessfully. timeout stops an overlong formatter. unsupported marks a file or operation outside the supported subset.
Data location

The native database is under the Tauri application-data directory for dev.r-console.ide: Application Support on macOS, APPDATA on Windows, and XDG data on Linux. Back it up before manual recovery. Automated corruption recovery and diagnostics bundles remain pending.

title: Updates & limitations
summary: RTcode 0.1.0 is an early implementation, with explicit release gates still open.

blocks.text: Available in this build

Tauri/Solid workbench; Monaco tabs, editing, built-in TS/JS intelligence, JSON/CSS validation, HTML completion, and a Problems panel; native scoped tree and create; revision-checked UTF-8 save; native search; Git status, refs, history, staging, local switch and patch view; xterm PTY sessions and SSH launch; external formatter; SQLite preferences and trust; bundled searchable Guide.
Still to implement

External LSP brokerage, framework language plugins, continuous project file watching, VSIX inspection/install, file watcher and external-change comparison, Save As, explorer rename/trash UI, recovery buffers, recent-session restoration, SSH favorites/config handles, virtualized large lists, rich diff models, complete setting/action/error coverage, signed updater, release packaging, and performance gates.
Validation scope

Browser interaction and native checks on the development machine do not establish Windows or Linux support. IME, ConPTY, host-key prompts, signing, upgrades, process descendants, and all support-matrix requirements need packaged tests on real target systems.
Roadmap honesty
Web extensions and remote workspaces remain conditional. No Marketplace access, Node extension host, AI chat, debugger, or Git network controls are included.

title: Glossary
summary: The terms used throughout the workbench.

blocks.text: Workspace
A local folder and the scoped authority to operate on its files. Restricted Mode allows editing while blocking code execution.
PTY
A pseudoterminal: the native terminal interface that connects an interactive shell to xterm.js. xterm.js is the renderer, not a shell.
LSP
Language Server Protocol: a structured conversation between an editor and a language tool. Monaco alone does not supply a server.
Git and extensions

Staged changes are in Git’s index. A remote-tracking branch is a local record of a remote ref, not a live network connection. VSIX is an archive format, not proof of API compatibility. A capability limits what a webview can ask the native host to do.
